newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Meridor resignation threatens Israel coalition.
newsitem.headline: Meridor resignation threatens Israel coalition.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was in hot water with coalition partners on Thursday over the resignation of Finance Minister Dan Meridor.
A key immigrant party's hint that it could leave the coalition rang alarm bells in Netanyahu's ruling Likud party.

"Today the situation is that indeed anyone leaving or any shakeup in a party that's a partner in the coalition could lead to the fall of the government," Tourism Minister Moshe Katsav, of Likud, told Israel Radio on Thursday.
"Because of the statements by the coalition partners, like Sharansky last night, the concern has grown that the coalition is completely unstable and could fall in the vote," Katsav said.
Industry and Trade Minister Natan Sharansky told Israel Television on Wednesday night: "We are already, in effect, with one foot outside, we are already not part of the coalition."
The government coalition commands 66 seats in the 120-seat parliament. Sharansky's party has seven seats and could determine the government's fate.

Sharansky was referring to his Yisrael Ba-Aliya party members voting as they please for the last week in parliament to protest Netanyahu's not honouring commitments in their coalition agreement and his delay in adopting proposals Sharansky crafted with Meridor on improving the government.
Sharansky would not say whether his party would vote with the government in a no-confidence vote set for Tuesday.

But he and members of his party have said Netanyahu can still bring them back into the fold by adopting the proposals for better government, coming up with a comprehensive housing plan and honouring coalition agreements.
Meridor quit on Wednesday over currency reforms adopted by the cabinet in a hastily arranged night session.

Political commentators gave greater credence to Meridor's argument Netanyahu had "ulterior motives" and that he was forced out in a well-orchestrated campaign to consolidate the prime minister's hold over his Likud party.
Sharansky said he felt "lonelier" in government without Meridor. Meridor on Thursday hinted he might not show up for Tuesday's vote.
"On Tuesday? I must look in my diary. I can't tell you right now...Let's wait and see," Meridor responded when Israel Radio asked him if he would attend the no-confidence vote.

Sharansky was a Jewish dissident who battled the Soviet Union during nine years behind bars before coming to Israel in 1986. In 1996, he led a party of Russian immigrants in national elections, winning enough votes to act as kingmaker.
Meridor's resignation, which takes effect on Friday, was the latest controversy to shake Netanyahu's year-old administration but not the first to spur Sharansky to consider bolting.

Police this year recommended Netanyahu be indicted for fraud and breach of trust in the ill-fated appointment of an attorney general in January. Sharansky withdrew a threat to topple the government over the affair when prosecutors ruled in April that there was insufficient evidence to indict.

In early March, the National Religious Party (NRP) which champions Jewish settlement of occupied Arab lands, and hawkish members of Likud threatened to bring down the government unless Netanyahu began building a settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
On March 18, Netanyahu sent bulldozers to begin work, saving his government but plunging peacemaking with Palestinians into deep crisis which has persisted for three months.
The government holds its weekly meeting on Friday, at which the recommendations for better government could be adopted, defusing Sharansky's current threat.
